notes: Ruling slot 22 = Armed Forces of Honduras (Lopez Arellano). The real civilian partner, the National Party, sits in coalition slot 13 as the regime's party of power; slot 1 holds the Christian Democratic Movement. Liberal Party kept in MD slot 2. MD's Montes Clan (modern) replaced by COHEP in slot 15. Mancha Brava (National Party shock troops) placed in slot 20, CES political police in slot 7.

0.name: Tela Railroad Company
0.text:
The Tela Railroad Company is the Honduran subsidiary of the United Fruit Company, owner of vast banana plantations, railways and ports on the North Coast since the early twentieth century. Together with Standard Fruit, it has shaped Honduran politics for decades, financing caudillos and negotiating directly with presidents and generals.

The company favours stable, pliant governments, low taxes on banana exports and firm handling of strikes, and it relies on Washington's goodwill to protect its concessions. It has learned to live with unions since 1954 but fears land reform. Its leverage lies in jobs, export revenue and its ability to make or break the North Coast economy.

1.name: Movimiento Demócrata Cristiano de Honduras
1.text:
The Christian Democratic Movement of Honduras was founded in 1968 by Catholic activists, young professionals and organisers of the Church's rural programmes. It is not yet a registered party and cannot run candidates, but it is spreading through peasant leagues, cooperatives and the radio schools of the Church.

The movement calls for agrarian reform, cooperatives, honest elections and an end to the two-party system dominated by caudillos and generals. It is sympathetic to the United States' reformist rhetoric but critical of the fruit companies. Its leverage lies in Catholic networks in the countryside and in its appeal to a new generation tired of nationalists and liberals alike.

2.name: Partido Liberal de Honduras
2.text:
The Liberal Party of Honduras, founded in 1891, is one of the country's two historic parties. It was robbed of almost certain victory in 1963 when Oswaldo López Arellano seized power ten days before the elections, and its dominant figure, Modesto Rodas Alvarado, remains the regime's most prominent civilian critic.

The Liberals stand for constitutional government, civilian control of the military, public education and moderate social reform, and they have strong roots among urban workers and on the North Coast. They are pro-American. Their leverage lies in a mass following of red-banner loyalists, the labour movement and the regime's need for national unity after the 1969 war.

3.name: Confederación de Trabajadores de Honduras
3.text:
The Confederation of Honduran Workers was founded in 1964 and unites the strongest unions in Central America, above all the banana workers of the North Coast whose great strike of 1954 won them legal recognition. It is affiliated with the inter-American ORIT and supported by American labour advisers.

The CTH pursues collective bargaining, labour law enforcement, social security and gradual reform within a democratic, anti-communist framework. It is wary of the military but avoids open confrontation. Its leverage lies in tens of thousands of organised workers on the plantations and in San Pedro Sula, who can paralyse the export economy.

4.name: Partido Comunista de Honduras
4.text:
The Communist Party of Honduras was founded in 1954 amid the great banana strike and has been illegal for almost its entire existence. It operates underground, persecuted by the security forces since the 1963 coup, and it lost part of its youth to a Maoist split in 1967.

Loyal to Moscow, the PCH seeks a broad democratic and anti-imperialist front against the military and the fruit companies, working through unions, peasant groups and the university rather than armed struggle. Its leverage is limited to dedicated cadres in the labour movement and among students and teachers in Tegucigalpa and San Pedro Sula.

5.name: Federación de Estudiantes Universitarios de Honduras
5.native_full: Federación de Estudiantes Universitarios de Honduras
5.text:
The Federation of Honduran University Students represents students at the National Autonomous University in Tegucigalpa, where left-wing groups dominate campus politics. In 1970 it is a centre of opposition to the military, the fruit companies and the government's handling of the 1969 war.

The federation celebrates the Cuban Revolution, denounces US imperialism and debates whether Honduras needs a guerrilla front of its own. Its leverage lies in street protests, strikes that can close the capital's streets, and the campus as a sanctuary and recruiting ground for Marxist activists.

6.name: El Zuñiguismo
6.text:
Zúñiga's Machine is the hardline network built around Ricardo Zúñiga Augustinus, the National Party boss who serves as President López Arellano's right hand and controls patronage, appointments and the party apparatus. He is widely regarded as the most powerful civilian in the country.

The faction stands for uncompromising cachureco conservatism: no power-sharing with the Liberals, harsh treatment of unions and leftists, and elections managed to guarantee victory. It distrusts foreign reformers, including meddling American advisers. Its leverage lies in its grip on the state bureaucracy, the electoral machinery and the party's street enforcers.

7.name: Cuerpo Especial de Seguridad
7.text:
The Special Security Corps was created after the 1963 coup to replace the Liberal-dominated Civil Guard, which the army destroyed in bloody fighting. Under military command, it serves as national police and political police at once, watching the opposition, unions and the university.

The CES treats dissent as subversion and relies on informers, arrests and intimidation to keep the regime secure. It answers to the high command rather than to the courts or Congress. Its leverage lies in surveillance files, control of the streets and its role as the instrument that keeps the military regime in place.

8.name: Círculo de Tiro
8.text:
The Tyre Circle is a small group of Lebanese Shia families in San Pedro Sula and Tegucigalpa, part of the Levantine merchant community that dominates Honduran commerce. They gather for religious holidays and follow the work of Imam Musa al-Sadr in southern Lebanon, who has just founded the Supreme Islamic Shia Council.

The circle admires al-Sadr's call for education, social justice and the dignity of the poor, and it favours loyal integration in Honduras. It avoids politics, but its shops, import houses and remittances give it discreet economic weight in the North Coast business world.

9.name: La Senda de Qom
9.text:
The Path of Qom is a handful of devout young Shia of Lebanese descent who have studied abroad and brought back the sermons of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled in Najaf, and his lectures on government by the Islamic jurist. They meet quietly in private homes in San Pedro Sula.

The group condemns both the American and Soviet blocs and dreams of a revolutionary Islamic order led by the clergy. It has no prospects in Honduras and is regarded with alarm by the community's elders, but its zeal and foreign contacts make it a potential channel for outside influence.

10.name: Los Peregrinos de San Pedro Sula
10.english: The Pilgrims of San Pedro Sula
10.native_full: Los Peregrinos de San Pedro Sula
10.text:
The Pilgrims of San Pedro Sula are a small association of Sunni Muslim merchants of Palestinian origin who have made the pilgrimage to Mecca and keep up contacts with the Muslim World League. They organise communal prayers, religious instruction and charity within an overwhelmingly Christian Arab community.

The group preaches piety, obedience to rulers and moral conservatism and shares the government's hostility to communism. Its leverage lies in commercial wealth, respectability among the North Coast business elite and connections to Saudi patrons.

11.name: La Célula del Califato
11.text:
The Caliphate Cell is a tiny clandestine group of young Muslims of Palestinian descent who discovered the ideas of Hizb ut-Tahrir while studying in Jordan. They read Taqiuddin al-Nabhani's writings on the restoration of the caliphate and maintain irregular contact with sympathisers abroad.

The cell rejects nationalism, democracy and both superpowers and calls for a single Islamic state uniting all Muslims. It has no base in Honduras, but it is secretive, disciplined and determined to spread its message among the young.

12.name: Hermanos de la Costa Norte
12.text:
The Brothers of the North Coast are a small study circle of educated Muslims of Arab descent in San Pedro Sula and La Ceiba who read Hassan al-Banna and Sayyid Qutb and follow the fortunes of the Muslim Brotherhood in Egypt and Jordan. Most are professionals or students.

The circle advocates personal piety, mutual aid and an Islamic social order built through education and charity, keeping its distance from both superpowers. Its influence is minimal, limited to community welfare and religious instruction within the small Muslim minority.

13.name: Partido Nacional de Honduras
13.text:
The National Party of Honduras, founded in 1902, is the party of the late dictator Tiburcio Carías Andino and the civilian partner of the military regime. It backed López Arellano's 1963 coup and dominated the 1965 constituent assembly that made him constitutional president, and its apparatus is run by Ricardo Zúñiga Augustinus.

The Nationalists stand for order, anti-communism, rural conservatism and the authority of the state, and they are firmly aligned with the United States. Their base lies in the countryside, among landowners, small farmers and public employees. Their leverage comes from control of the bureaucracy, patronage and the electoral machinery.

14.name: Federación Nacional de Agricultores y Ganaderos de Honduras
14.english: National Federation of Farmers and Ranchers of Honduras
14.native_full: Federación Nacional de Agricultores y Ganaderos de Honduras
14.text:
The National Federation of Farmers and Ranchers of Honduras was founded in 1966 by cattle ranchers and commercial farmers expanding into the southern and eastern lowlands. It campaigned loudly for the eviction of Salvadoran settlers, helping to inflame the tensions that led to the 1969 war.

FENAGH defends private landownership, opposes agrarian reform and peasant land occupations, and demands credit and roads for commercial agriculture. Its conservatism is rooted in the countryside rather than in bloc politics. Its leverage lies in landed wealth, ties to local military commanders and influence in the National Party.

15.name: Consejo Hondureño de la Empresa Privada
15.native_full: Consejo Hondureño de la Empresa Privada
15.text:
The Honduran Council of Private Enterprise was founded in 1967 to unite the chambers of commerce, industry, agriculture and banking in a single voice. It speaks for the family business groups of Tegucigalpa and San Pedro Sula, many of them of Arab and immigrant origin.

COHEP defends free enterprise, low taxation and the Central American Common Market, damaged by the 1969 war, and it opposes radical agrarian reform and union militancy. Its leverage lies in investment, credit and direct access to the president and the ministers who manage the economy.

16.name: Cámara de Comercio e Industrias de Cortés
16.english: Chamber of Commerce and Industries of Cortés
16.native_full: Cámara de Comercio e Industrias de Cortés
16.text:
The Chamber of Commerce and Industries of Cortés, founded in 1931 in San Pedro Sula, represents the dynamic merchants and manufacturers of the North Coast, the country's commercial heart. Its members resent the centralism of Tegucigalpa and the weight of the state.

The chamber champions free trade, open ports, low tariffs and minimal bureaucracy, and it looks to the United States as its main market and partner. Its base is the business community of San Pedro Sula, and its leverage lies in trade, employment and the economic weight of the North Coast.

17.name: Guardianes de La Tigra
17.text:
The Guardians of La Tigra are a loose group of foresters, university naturalists and teachers in Tegucigalpa concerned about the cloud forest above the capital, which supplies much of its water. Logging, mining and land clearing are eating into the forests of La Tigra and the pine woods of the interior.

They call for protected reserves, reforestation, control of logging concessions and safe water for the capital. They avoid party politics and bloc rivalries. Their leverage is small, resting on scientific credibility, the press and the self-interest of a capital city that fears running dry.

18.name: Asociación Nacional de Campesinos de Honduras
18.native_full: Asociación Nacional de Campesinos de Honduras
18.text:
The National Association of Honduran Peasants was founded in 1962 and has grown into the largest peasant organisation in the country, with roots among former banana workers on the North Coast. In 1970 it presses the government to distribute the land left vacant by the expulsion of Salvadoran settlers.

ANACH demands agrarian reform, peasant cooperatives, credit and an end to the power of ranchers and fruit companies over land. It works through organised land occupations and negotiations with the National Agrarian Institute. Its leverage lies in tens of thousands of members who can mobilise across the countryside.

19.name: Partido Comunista de Honduras (Marxista-Leninista)
19.text:
The Communist Party of Honduras (Marxist-Leninist) broke away from the pro-Moscow PCH in 1967, rejecting its cautious line in favour of the Chinese model. It is a small underground organisation of students, teachers and young militants, persecuted by the security forces.

The party denounces Soviet revisionism and American imperialism alike and calls for a people's war based on the peasantry to overthrow the military and the fruit companies. Its leverage is limited to student circles at the National University and scattered rural contacts, but its radicalism attracts impatient young activists.

20.name: La Mancha Brava
20.text:
La Mancha Brava is the notorious band of National Party street enforcers that has broken up Liberal rallies, intimidated voters and harassed opponents since the 1963 coup. During the crisis of 1969 its members were prominent in the violent campaign against Salvadoran settlers.

The group thrives on xenophobic nationalism, cachureco loyalty and hostility toward Liberals, leftists and Salvadorans, and it sees itself as the defender of the Honduran people against foreigners and traitors. Its leverage lies in muscle, patronage from party bosses and impunity granted by the authorities.

21.name: Los Cariístas
21.text:
The Cariístas are the old guard who served under Tiburcio Carías Andino, dictator of Honduras from 1933 to 1949, who died in December 1969. Veteran politicians, rural bosses and retired officers, they still nostalgically recall the iron years of 'encierro, destierro y entierro' for opponents.

They favour a single strongman, the suppression of the Liberals and the left, censorship and rural order enforced by local commanders, viewing democracy as a source of chaos. Their numbers are dwindling, but their prestige within the National Party and their ties to rural caudillos still carry weight.

22.name: Fuerzas Armadas de Honduras
22.text:
The Armed Forces of Honduras have ruled the country since General Oswaldo López Arellano overthrew President Ramón Villeda Morales in October 1963. López Arellano, confirmed as constitutional president in 1965, remains both head of state and commander of the armed forces, though the army's poor showing in the 1969 war has damaged its prestige.

The military presents itself as the guardian of national order and anti-communism, closely tied to the United States through aid and training. It governs in partnership with the National Party. Its leverage lies in the guns, the security forces and the constitutional autonomy that places the commander beyond civilian control.

23.name: Los Leales del Rey Mosco
23.text:
The Loyalists of the Mosquito King are Miskito elders and community leaders in the remote department of Gracias a Dios who keep alive the memory of the Mosquito Kingdom, once protected by Britain, whose kings ruled the Caribbean coast until the late nineteenth century. Moravian church networks preserve its stories and customs.

They seek recognition of communal lands, Miskito language and traditional authority, and they distrust the distant governments in Tegucigalpa. Their influence is local and cultural, but they command loyalty in villages that the Honduran state barely reaches.
